items.title: Caesar's assassins included his own protégés
items.claim: Who killed Julius Caesar on 15 March 44 BCE?

options.text: A conspiracy of around 60 senators, led by Marcus Junius Brutus (who Caesar had pardoned and promoted) and Gaius Cassius Longinus, stabbed him 23 times in Pompey's Theatre
Mark Antony alone, in a private quarrel
He died of natural causes; the assassination is a later invention

items.reveal:
Caesar had crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BCE, defeated Pompey at Pharsalus (48), and been declared dictator perpetuo in February 44 BCE. The conspirators feared a return to monarchy.

The assassination took place at a Senate meeting at the Curia of Pompey. Suetonius and Plutarch describe the scene; the famous 'Et tu, Brute?' is Shakespeare's. Plutarch records Caesar saying 'kai su, teknon?' ('you too, child?') in Greek to Brutus.

The Liberators expected to restore the Republic. Instead they triggered the Liberators' civil war, ending at Philippi (42 BCE) with Brutus's suicide. Octavian became Augustus, first emperor, in 27 BCE — the Republic was over.
items.why: Assassinations rarely produce the political outcome the assassins want. The Liberators killed to save the Republic and accelerated its end — a paradox of political violence visible across history.

items.title: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE but converted slowly
items.claim: When did the Roman Empire become Christian?

options.text: Constantine made Christianity the state religion in 312

The Edict of Milan (313) granted religious toleration; Constantine increasingly favoured Christianity but was baptised only on his deathbed in 337; Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion by the Edict of Thessalonica in 380
The empire remained pagan until 600 CE

items.reveal:
Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312) over Maxentius came after a reported vision of the Chi-Rho symbol with 'in hoc signo vinces' (in this sign you will conquer). The Edict of Milan, agreed with Licinius in 313, granted religious toleration to all.

Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea (325) and built churches across the empire. He moved the capital to Constantinople (founded 330). He was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by an Arian bishop, Eusebius of Nicomedia.

The Edict of Thessalonica (380) under Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion. Pagan worship was progressively restricted; the Olympic Games were banned in 393.
items.why: Religious change at imperial scale is a process, not a moment. The 67 years between Milan and Thessalonica saw a tolerant empire become a Christian one — a transformation studied by every subsequent religious-political shift.

items.title: WWI was triggered by a wrong turn
items.claim: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand survived the first assassination attempt that morning. What caused the second, successful attempt hours later?

options.text: A coordinated second wave of assassins ambushed his motorcade on the way to the hospital
His driver took a wrong turn into a side street, stalled the car, and stopped directly in front of Gavrilo Princip
Princip followed the motorcade by tram and intercepted it at the town hall
A Serbian double agent inside the security detail signalled his location

items.reveal_title: A wrong turn into world war
items.reveal:
After a bomb attack that morning failed, the Archduke insisted on visiting the wounded at the hospital. His driver, Leopold Lojka, had not been told the route had been changed. He turned right onto Franz Joseph Street, was told he was going the wrong way, and stalled while reversing.

Gavrilo Princip, who had given up and was eating a sandwich (the sandwich story is disputed but he was at Schiller's delicatessen), happened to be standing there. He stepped forward and fired twice from five feet away.
items.why: The 'causes of WWI' essay tends to load every variable onto structural forces (alliances, militarism, imperialism). Those forces created the powder keg, but a stalled car lit the fuse. Contingency matters.
